It is a review rather than a trial, so use it to recognise patterns and to see how the cosmetic cause is distinguished from infectious and inflammatory mimics.

visual.title: Nail cross-section with a contact boundary and a referral gate
visual.description: A step sequence that maps the plate and the surrounding skin, marks where monomer sits and where risk begins, and places a clinical gate at the findings a cosmetic routine cannot explain.
steps: Step 1, plate: draw the nail plate as a thick keratin sheet and label it a good barrier, noting that high monomer concentrations are accepted here provided the surface is intact.
Step 2, margin: draw the cuticle and nail fold as thin skin, label it the site of contact, and mark that the safety proviso depends on product staying off this band.
Step 3, cure layer: show the ultraviolet lamp above the plate and mark under-cured margins, where unreacted monomer remains and filing produces contaminated debris.
Step 4, transfer arrow: draw an arrow from the fingertips to the eyelids and label it hand transfer, with the note that dermatitis at a distance is still contact dermatitis.
Step 5, clinical findings: list onycholysis, nail fold inflammation, pain, paraesthesia and a single dystrophic nail beside a gate labelled clinician, because these are not cosmetic variations.

Step 6, label check: attach a box naming hydroxyethyl methacrylate, methyl methacrylate, formalin, methylene glycol and toluenesulfonamide formaldehyde resin, and note that hypoallergenic carries no legal definition.

lessons.title: Lips: a transitional surface, not a thin version of the face
lessons.explanation: The lip is the one part of the face that is better understood as a boundary than as an area of skin. The vermilion, the coloured part, is a transition zone between facial skin and the oral mucosa: it is hairless, highly vascularised and covered by a non-keratinised lamellar squamous epithelium. A 2025 review of lip ageing gives the numbers that make the practical difference. The epithelium of the vermilion contains three to five cellular layers, against approximately sixteen in typical facial skin, and the vermilion lacks the usual skin appendages, meaning hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands. The redness is a consequence of the same anatomy: less melanin, a thinner epithelium and a dense capillary bed beneath it. Two further findings from the same literature change how a learner should think about lip products. The ceramide profile of the lip differs from other skin sites, with lower total ceramide content, a higher proportion of short-chain ceramide species and a higher share of particular ceramide classes, and the fatty acid composition of the vermilion shows higher accumulation of docosahexaenoic acid than other skin. A thin epithelium with a different lipid mixture and no sebaceous film is a surface that loses water quickly and has little reserve when it is challenged. That single sentence explains most of what people notice about their lips. Because there are no sebaceous glands, the surface film depends entirely on what is applied and on what the mouth does. Occlusion therefore works: petrolatum and similar hydrocarbons reduce water loss and give the epithelium time to recover, which is the same mechanism lesson 33 described for the face, applied to a surface with less margin. A humectant without an occlusive is a different proposition here, because drawing water into a thin epithelium that loses it rapidly can leave the surface feeling drier once the humidity falls, which is exactly the ambient humidity caveat from the earlier lesson. Licking is the third mechanism and the most underrated. Saliva evaporates and takes heat with it, the enzymes and salts in it are mildly irritating, and the tongue is a mechanical challenge, so a learner who licks her lips because they feel dry creates the dryness she is trying to relieve. The result is a cycle that looks like dependence on a balm and is better described as dependence on occlusion, since the balm is the only thing interrupting it. Two clinical boundaries belong in the same lesson. The first is angular cheilitis, fissuring and maceration at the corners of the mouth, which has causes a balm cannot address: candidal infection, nutritional deficiency, loss of vertical dimension in denture wearers, and irritation from saliva pooling. The second is a persistent lesion on the lip itself. The lower lip accumulates ultraviolet exposure over a lifetime and is a common site for actinic cheilitis and squamous cell carcinoma, so a crusted, ulcerated or non-healing area, particularly one that bleeds, is an examination rather than a cosmetic problem. Ultraviolet protection for the lip is therefore not a marketing extra. It is a drug claim in the United States when the product carries an SPF, and the practical requirement is the same as elsewhere: enough product, reapplied, and a formula a person will actually use.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner has applied a strawberry-flavoured balm more than ten times a day for six weeks. Her lips peel in sheets, feel tight after each application wears off, and the corners are fissured and sore. She believes her lips have become addicted to the balm. Work through the mechanisms in order. Step one, the occlusion cycle. The balm contains petrolatum, so it reduces water loss while it is present; when it wears off, the thin epithelium loses water faster than facial skin would, and the contrast is felt as worsening. That is physics, not addiction. Step two, the flavouring. Cinnamal, menthol and similar flavour compounds are recognised irritants and potential allergens in lip products, and a flavoured balm applied ten times a day delivers a repeated dose to a surface with three to five cell layers. The peeling in sheets is consistent with a low-grade contact reaction superimposed on dryness. Step three, the licking. Ask directly. Most learners with this pattern lick their lips without noticing, particularly in dry indoor air, and the evaporation of saliva reproduces the symptom within minutes. Step four, the corners. Fissuring at the commissures moves the problem out of the cosmetic category, because candidal colonisation, iron or B vitamin deficiency, and denture-related loss of vertical dimension are all treatable causes that a balm will not resolve. Step five, the plan. Stop the flavoured product, switch to plain petrolatum or a simple ointment, add a lip product with sun protection for daytime outdoor use, stop licking by substituting water and a conscious swallow, and set a review point at two to three weeks. If the corners have not healed, or if any area ulcerates or bleeds, the next step is a clinician and not a stronger balm. Step six, the expectation. Barrier recovery on the lip takes days to weeks rather than hours, and the improvement is felt before it is visible, so the learner should judge the change by the number of applications needed per day rather than by appearance alone.
lessons.question: A learner has a crusted, slightly bleeding area on the lower lip that has been present for eight weeks. She has been exfoliating it with a sugar scrub and applying a peppermint balm. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: A lip lesion that persists for weeks, crusts or bleeds needs clinical examination, because the differential includes actinic cheilitis and squamous cell carcinoma, and mechanical exfoliation delays diagnosis
lessons.distractor: The crust is thickened dead skin from a damaged barrier, so weekly exfoliation and a medicated balm will resolve it once the surface turns over
lessons.correction: The lower lip is a high ultraviolet accumulation site and a common location for premalignant and malignant change, and the features that separate a cosmetic problem from a clinical one are persistence, crusting, ulceration, bleeding and failure to heal with bland occlusion. Exfoliating such an area adds trauma and removes the surface that a clinician needs to see. The lip vermilion has only three to five epithelial layers, no appendages and a lipid profile with more short-chain ceramides, so it is poorly equipped to tolerate scrubs, menthol and peppermint oil. The appropriate advice is to stop the irritants, use plain occlusion and sun protection, and have the lesion examined, without suggesting a diagnosis.

depth.definitions: Vermilion: the red, keratinised transition zone of the lip between skin and oral mucosa. Commissure: the corner of the mouth where the upper and lower lips meet. Cheilitis: inflammation of the lip. Angular cheilitis: fissuring and maceration at the commissure, with infective, nutritional and mechanical causes. Actinic cheilitis: ultraviolet-induced change of the lip that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Exfoliative cheilitis: persistent scaling and peeling of the lip without an identifiable external cause. Ceramide: a family of sphingolipids that form part of the intercellular lipid matrix of the stratum corneum. Occlusive: a substance that reduces water loss by forming a film. Humectant: a substance that binds water. Period after opening: the labelled interval, in months, during which an opened product is expected to remain stable.
depth.mechanism: Three structural facts produce the behaviour. A three to five layer epithelium offers a short diffusion path and little reservoir, so water leaves quickly and applied substances reach viable tissue with less hindrance than on the cheek. The absence of sebaceous glands removes the endogenous lipid film that on the face limits water loss, which is why the lip depends on applied occlusion rather than on its own secretion. The ceramide profile, with lower total content and a higher proportion of short-chain species, produces a less ordered intercellular matrix, so the barrier is both thinner and chemically weaker. Saliva adds a fourth factor: evaporation of the water film cools the surface and, in dry air, removes water from the epithelium, while salivary enzymes and salts produce mild irritation, and repeated wetting and drying disrupts whatever lipid remains. The clinical consequence is that occlusion interrupts the cycle at the water loss step, barrier repair follows over days, and any intervention that adds friction or a sensitiser works against recovery.
depth.secondExample: Consider a learner who wants to apply her prescription retinoid to her lips because the tube says it improves texture and the lips look lined. This is a category error with a predictable outcome. The retinoid was assessed for facial skin with a stratum corneum of roughly sixteen layers, and the lip has three to five layers, no appendages and a different lipid matrix, so the same concentration produces a much larger effective dose per unit of viable tissue. Irritation on the lip presents as peeling, fissuring and soreness that mimics the dryness the learner was trying to treat, and because the lip is in constant contact with saliva and with food, the product is also partly removed and partly ingested. The correct transfer is not from face to lip but from the lip's own requirements: occlusion, ultraviolet protection, and avoidance of irritants and allergens. A second learner makes the mirror error, applying a strong exfoliating acid to the lip to remove peeling, which produces the same fissuring by a different route. Both errors come from treating the lip as a small face.
depth.mistake: The two errors are mirror images. The first is to treat lip dryness as a product deficiency and escalate through flavoured balms, scrubs and acids, when the mechanisms at work are water loss, licking and irritation, all of which escalation worsens. The second is to treat a persistent lip lesion as dryness, when persistence, crusting, ulceration and bleeding are the features that make it a clinical question. Underneath both sits the assumption that the lip is simply thinner facial skin, which is why the wrong product categories get chosen. The diagnostic correction is a three-line history: what is applied and how often, what the mouth does (licking, biting, sucking), and how long the finding has been present without healing. The first two are cosmetic variables, the third is the trigger for referral.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Keep a seven-day lip diary recording every product applied, the number of applications per day, the number of times you notice licking or biting, and the indoor humidity or heating situation. At the end, write two sentences: the single change most likely to reduce water loss, and the finding that would make you seek assessment rather than adjust a product. Marking guide: a strong diary separates occlusion from humectancy, notices a flavoured or medicated product used more than a few times a day, and names a concrete review point such as two to three weeks. It should state a stop rule for ulceration, bleeding or a lesion that has not healed. A diary that concludes the lips are simply dry has not yet met the standard.
depth.summary: The lip vermilion is a transition zone with three to five epithelial layers, no hair follicles, sweat or sebaceous glands, and a ceramide profile shifted towards short-chain species, so it loses water quickly and depends on applied occlusion. That explains frequent reapplication without any need to invoke addiction, and it explains why licking, flavouring and exfoliation all worsen the problem. Angular fissuring and any lip lesion that persists, crusts or bleeds are clinical findings, with actinic change on the lower lip among the reasons. Occlusion and ultraviolet protection are the two interventions the anatomy supports.

readings.title: Aging of the Human Lip: Current Knowledge and Clinical Implications (2025, PMC)
readings.note: Read the introduction and the structural description for the three to five epithelial layers of the vermilion against roughly sixteen in facial skin, the absence of hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands, and the ceramide and fatty acid differences. It is a narrative review of more than 120 studies, so treat the specific figures as reported summaries rather than as measurements from a single cohort.

readings.title: Wertz (2021), Roles of Lipids in the Permeability Barriers of Skin and Oral Mucosa, International Journal of Molecular Sciences (PMC)
readings.note: Read the abstract and the comparison of epidermal and oral epithelial barriers, particularly the statement that oral keratinised epithelium contains a similar lipid mixture in lower amounts and is accordingly more permeable. Use it to understand why a surface with less lipid barrier depends on occlusion, and note that the paper focuses on skin and oral mucosa rather than on the vermilion specifically.

readings.title: StatPearls, Cheilitis (NCBI Bookshelf)
readings.note: Read the sections on angular, actinic, exfoliative and contact cheilitis for the differential and for the features that distinguish them. This is a clinical reference written for practitioners, so use it to recognise when a finding needs assessment, not to attempt a diagnosis. Bookshelf pages render for browsers and may return partial text to automated clients.

visual.title: Lip cross-section from occlusion to referral
visual.description: A step sequence that builds the vermilion from its layers outward, attaches each structural fact to a product behaviour, and ends with the findings that move a learner from cosmetic management to assessment.
steps: Step 1, layers: draw the vermilion as three to five cell layers above a capillary bed, and write the facial comparison of about sixteen layers beside it.
Step 2, appendages: mark the absence of hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands, and note that there is therefore no endogenous surface lipid film.
Step 3, lipid matrix: annotate the epithelium with lower total ceramides and a higher proportion of short-chain species, and label the result a weaker, thinner barrier.
Step 4, water loss and behaviour: add two arrows, one outward for water loss and one circular for licking, with the note that evaporation and salivary enzymes reproduce the dryness.

Step 5, product layer: place an occlusive film over the surface and label it the intervention that interrupts the cycle, then place a humectant-only product beside it and mark the low-humidity caveat.

Step 6, referral gate: draw a line at the commissure and at any persistent lesion, listing fissuring at the corners, ulceration, bleeding and eight weeks without healing as findings that belong to a clinician.

questions.prompt: A learner reads that an emulsifier in her moisturiser is 'banned in Europe' and concludes that the product, bought in the United States, must be unsafe. She asks whether she should throw it away. What is the accurate reading of the claim?
questions.answer: The claim needs the specific substance, its concentration and its legal status checked, because a prohibited-list entry is not the same as a measured risk and the two systems differ in both directions, with the EU permitting 29 UV filters against 17 in the United States
questions.distractor: Because the European Union prohibits more substances than the United States, any product sold in the United States contains more hazardous ingredients and should be replaced
questions.correction: A prohibition is a legal category, not a toxicological measurement, and the lists are not nested. Annex II of the EU regulation is a long list of prohibited substances, but popular 'banned in Europe' claims often cite entries that are substance classes, impurities or ingredients no longer used, and the traffic runs the other way too: the EU permits 29 UV filters while the United States monograph contains 17, so 18 filters available in Europe are not available in America. The decision-relevant question is which substance, at what concentration, in which product, used on which site. Replacing a product because of a slogan substitutes a legal category for an exposure assessment.

questions.prompt: A learner with melasma in the United Kingdom buys a United States sunscreen labelled SPF 50, broad spectrum, because it is half the price of her usual European product. She wants to know whether the protection is equivalent. What is the best appraisal?
questions.answer: The SPF number is comparable but the UVA signal is not: United States broad spectrum is defined by a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm without a required UVA protection factor ratio, while the European frame requires a UVA protection factor of at least one third of the SPF and a label to show it
questions.distractor: SPF 50 means the same protection in both markets, because sun protection factor is an international standard measured the same way everywhere
questions.correction: The in vivo SPF test is standardised internationally, so the UVB number travels reasonably well. The UVA requirement does not. The United States broad-spectrum test asks whether the absorbance curve reaches 370 nm at 90 per cent of its area, a shape criterion, whereas the European recommendation requires a measured UVA protection factor of at least one third of the labelled SPF. For a pigmentary condition driven substantially by UVA and visible light, that difference is the one that matters, and a tinted formula containing iron oxides addresses visible light in a way that neither number captures.

questions.prompt: A learner with moderate inflammatory acne wants to buy a home blue-light mask instead of the topical her clinician suggested, citing the mask's 'FDA approval' and a study in which 86 per cent of participants improved by at least one grade. How should this be assessed?
questions.answer: Devices are cleared rather than approved, the cited study was a 7-week open-label sponsor-funded series of 30 participants, and the systematic review behind home LED use pooled six trials of short duration, so the mask is a possible adjunct rather than a replacement for treatment of moderate acne
questions.distractor: A clearance from the FDA establishes that the device works, and an 86 per cent response rate is high enough to replace a topical treatment
questions.correction: Clearance is a substantial-equivalence finding against a predicate device, not a demonstration of clinical superiority, and the 86 per cent figure comes from an open-label study of 30 people aged 14 to 45 with mild or moderate acne, funded by the device manufacturer, with no control arm and a seven-week horizon. The 2025 meta-analysis included six randomised trials with treatment durations from two days to twelve weeks, which is short for a condition that fluctuates over months. Blue light has a plausible antibacterial mechanism through porphyrin excitation, which is why it is worth discussing as an adjunct, but moderate acne is a clinical problem and the mask is not a substitute.

questions.prompt: After two years of gel manicures a learner develops itchy, red nail folds, lifting of two nail plates and a patch of eczema on both eyelids. She plans to switch to a 'hypoallergenic' gel brand. What is the correct reading?
questions.answer: The distribution suggests methacrylate allergy with ectopic transfer from fingers to eyelids, 'hypoallergenic' gels may still contain hydroxyethyl methacrylate, and this needs patch testing and avoidance rather than a brand change
questions.distractor: The eyelid eczema is unrelated to the nails because the products were never applied near the eyes, so the problem is probably a facial moisturiser
questions.correction: Methacrylates are contact allergens and the hands are a classic transfer route to the face, which is why eyelid dermatitis in a nail-product user is a recognised pattern rather than a coincidence. The SCCS opinion on HEMA and di-HEMA-TMHDC concluded that high concentrations on the nail plate are unlikely to sensitise provided contact with adjacent skin is avoided, which places the risk precisely at the cuticle and nail fold where uncured monomer sits. Hypoallergenic is a marketing word without a legal definition, and a 2025 report documented allergy to gel polishes sold under that description. Patch testing identifies the sensitiser and matters beyond cosmetics, because dental and orthopaedic methacrylates share the chemistry.

questions.prompt: A learner has applied a flavoured lip balm more than ten times a day for six weeks. Her lips peel, the corners are fissured and she reports that stopping the balm makes the dryness worse within a day. What is the appropriate plan?
questions.answer: Replace the flavoured balm with a plain occlusive and a lip product with sun protection, stop licking, and treat fissuring at the corners as a reason to see a clinician, because angular cheilitis has causes that a balm cannot address
questions.distractor: The worsening on stopping proves the lips have become dependent on the balm, so she should continue and add a second moisturising product to break the cycle
questions.correction: The lip vermilion has three to five cell layers against roughly sixteen in facial skin, no hair follicles, no sweat glands and no sebaceous glands, and a ceramide profile with more short-chain species, so it loses water quickly and depends on what is applied. That explains frequent reapplication without invoking addiction. Flavoured balms add potential irritants and allergens such as cinnamal and menthol, and licking adds evaporative loss and salivary enzymes. Fissuring at the commissures points to candidal, nutritional or dental causes, which is a clinical question, and a lesion that has not settled in six weeks needs examination rather than a stronger balm.

units.title: Clinical boundaries: itch, hair loss, pigment and light

lessons.title: Itch: the scratch cycle, and the point at which it stops being a cosmetic complaint
lessons.explanation: Itch is the most common symptom in dermatology and the one most often managed with a moisturiser for far too long. The definition has been stable for more than three centuries: an unpleasant sensation that provokes the urge or reflex to scratch. Duration is what changes its status. Acute itch is a protective reflex with an obvious cause; chronic pruritus is itch lasting more than six weeks, and a 2025 narrative review puts its prevalence at 8 to 25 per cent of the population, with estimates of about 15 per cent in children aged six to ten and about 25 per cent in people aged 65 and over. The same review reports that severe itch is associated with sleep disturbance, shame, depressed mood and anxiety, and that suicidal ideation was reported in 18.5 per cent of patients with chronic pruritus. That figure is worth pausing on, because it reframes itch from an annoyance to a symptom with measurable harm. The classification used by the International Forum for the Study of Itch separates three situations: itch on skin that is already lesional, where a skin disease is present; itch on skin that looks unchanged, historically called pruritus sine materia; and itch accompanied by severe scratch lesions such as prurigo or lichen simplex. The middle category is the one that matters most for a course about cosmetics, because there is nothing to see and therefore nothing for a product to target, while the underlying cause may be hepatic, renal, haematological, endocrine or pharmacological. Two mechanisms run in parallel. Histaminergic itch is the familiar pathway, mediated by histamine acting on sensory neurons, and it is the minority of chronic cases. Non-histaminergic itch involves other mediators and receptors, including interleukin 31 and the type 2 cytokines interleukin 4 and interleukin 13, which is why antihistamines so often fail and why the newer biologic and Janus kinase inhibitor treatments were developed. Superimposed on both is the scratch cycle. Scratching damages the barrier, releases inflammatory mediators and sensitises nerve endings, so the threshold for the next itch falls and the response to it becomes more vigorous. A learner who scratches because the skin is dry makes the skin drier and more reactive, and a learner whose itch has a systemic cause still damages the skin on top of it. The cosmetic contribution is real but narrow. Emollients and occlusives reduce water loss and restore the barrier, which lowers the itch of xerosis, and the review lists emollients as the general measure applied before targeted treatment. What a cosmetic cannot do is diagnose. A soothing claim is also unusually hard to substantiate, because itch is a sensation rather than a surface property: it is measured by validated patient-reported scales such as a worst itch numerical rating scale, not by a corneometer, and a product that improves a biophysical reading has not shown that it reduces itch. The safety boundary is therefore a set of red flags rather than a diagnosis. Generalised itch with no rash, itch that disturbs sleep, itch with weight loss, night sweats or fever, itch with jaundice or dark urine, itch in an older person with no skin findings, itch that begins after a new medicine, and itch in pregnancy all point away from a cosmetic explanation and toward assessment. In each case the appropriate action is to keep the skin comfortable while arranging that assessment, not to escalate products.
lessons.example: Worked example. Two learners describe itching, and the difference between them decides everything. The first is 68, has had generalised itch for three months, worse at night, with no rash that she can see, and has tried three body lotions including an oat-based cream. The second is 34, has itchy, scaly shins each winter, and finds that a thick ointment used after showering settles it within a week. Begin with the first. Her itch is chronic by duration, generalised by distribution, and non-lesional by examination, which places it in the category where systemic causes are most likely and where the skin offers no clue. The relevant history is weight loss, fever, night sweats, new medicines, alcohol intake, jaundice, urinary change, and any known liver, kidney or thyroid disease. None of those questions can be answered by a product, and the investigation the review describes is a medical history, examination and laboratory testing, sometimes with imaging and biopsy. Her emollient is supportive care, and continuing it while she arranges assessment is reasonable. Continuing it as a twelve-week trial instead of arranging assessment is the failure. Now the second learner. Her itch is seasonal, localised to areas with visible xerosis, and responds to occlusion, which is the pattern of dry skin. The mechanism is water loss from a barrier that is deficient in lipids, and the intervention is an occlusive applied to damp skin after a short, lukewarm shower, with a reduced frequency of foaming cleanser. The distinction between the two cases is not the intensity of the itch, which may be similar, but duration, distribution, the presence of lesions and the response to occlusion. Write those four items down for any itch presentation and the decision usually makes itself.
lessons.question: A learner reports generalised itching for three months with no visible rash, worse at night, and asks which soothing lotion to buy next after three have failed. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Chronic generalised itch on apparently unchanged skin is a recognised clinical category with systemic causes, so she needs assessment and appropriate tests while emollients are used for comfort
lessons.distractor: Itch without a rash means dry skin, so the correct step is a thicker occlusive applied twice daily for eight to twelve weeks before considering anything else
lessons.correction: Itch on non-lesional skin is a distinct category in the International Forum for the Study of Itch classification precisely because a skin disease may be absent while a systemic one is present. The differential includes hepatic, renal, haematological, endocrine and drug-related causes, and the 2025 review describes assessment based on history, examination, laboratory testing and sometimes imaging or biopsy. Nocturnal generalised itch in an older person is a pattern that warrants that assessment rather than a longer cosmetic trial. Emollients remain appropriate comfort care and are listed as the general measure before targeted treatment, but they are not a diagnostic strategy, and treating them as one is how a diagnosis is delayed.

depth.definitions: Pruritus: an unpleasant sensation that provokes the urge to scratch. Chronic pruritus: itch lasting more than six weeks. Prurigo: a condition of itchy nodules produced by chronic scratching. Lichen simplex: thickened, lichenified skin resulting from repeated rubbing. Xerosis: dry skin, with reduced water content and a disrupted barrier. Histaminergic itch: itch mediated by histamine acting on sensory neurons. Non-histaminergic itch: itch driven by other mediators, including interleukin 31 and type 2 cytokines. Numerical rating scale: a patient-reported score, commonly the worst itch over 24 hours on a zero to ten scale. Emollient: a product that softens and smooths the skin and reduces water loss. Pruritus sine materia: the older term for itch without visible skin change.
depth.mechanism: Itch signals travel on dedicated sensory fibres to the spinal cord and brain, and the pathways are not a single channel. Histamine, released from mast cells, activates a subset of neurons and produces a histaminergic itch that responds partly to antihistamines. Interleukin 31, released by T cells and other sources, acts on its own receptor complex on sensory neurons and produces a non-histaminergic itch that antihistamines do not touch, which is why the type 2 cytokine axis became a drug target. Scratching adds a second loop: mechanical injury releases adenosine triphosphate and other mediators, lowers the activation threshold of nerve endings, and produces the flare and wheal that make the skin more sensitive. In xerotic skin the starting point is barrier failure. Reduced intercellular lipid, lower water content and a thicker, less flexible stratum corneum produce microcracks that expose nerve endings and allow irritants in. Occlusion restores water content, reduces the cracks and lowers the sensory input, which is a mechanical explanation for a clinical improvement rather than a pharmacological one.
depth.secondExample: Consider a learner who develops itch three weeks after starting a new medicine for blood pressure, with no rash and no change in her skincare. The temporal relationship is the only clue, and it is a good one: drug-related itch can appear without a visible eruption, and the list of medicines associated with photosensitivity and with pruritus overlaps only partly, so the two questions are different. Her cosmetic routine is irrelevant to the cause, and adding a soothing product changes nothing except her expenditure. The correct action is to bring the medicine list, with start dates, to the prescriber, and not to stop the medicine herself, because an antihypertensive stopped abruptly can produce a worse problem than the itch. Compare her with a learner whose itch began when she started a new foaming cleanser on her legs, is confined to the areas she washes, and settles when she stops: that is an irritant contact pattern, the mechanism is surfactant disruption of the lipid barrier from lesson 32, and the intervention is a product change. Same symptom, two different questions: what changed internally, and what changed externally.
depth.mistake: The dominant error is to treat itch as a synonym for dryness, which converts every presentation into a moisturiser problem and delays the ones that are not. The second error is to use antihistamines as a diagnostic test, reasoning that if an antihistamine helps, the cause was allergic, when most chronic itch is non-histaminergic and a partial response proves little. The third is to escalate products in response to scratching, which treats the visible damage rather than the sensation and often adds irritants to a barrier that is already compromised. The diagnostic correction is a four-item summary written before any product is chosen: how long, how widespread, is there a primary lesion, and does occlusion help. Duration beyond six weeks and generalised distribution without lesions are the two items that most reliably move a learner from the cosmetic aisle to a clinic.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. For one week, record a daily worst itch score from zero to ten, the body areas involved, whether any rash or scratch mark was visible, and what was applied. At the end, write four lines matching the lesson's summary items and one sentence naming the red flag, if any, that would make you seek assessment. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong record distinguishes a primary lesion from a scratch mark, notes night-time worsening and sleep disturbance, and correctly identifies that a generalised itch without rash is not explained by a product. An entry that records only the products tried does not yet meet the standard, because the pattern is the finding.
depth.summary: Chronic pruritus lasts more than six weeks, affects an estimated 8 to 25 per cent of the population and about a quarter of people over 65, and carries a measurable psychological burden. Itch on non-lesional skin is its own category with systemic causes, and the mediators are only partly histaminergic, which is why antihistamines often fail. The scratch cycle converts a sensation into barrier damage and further sensitisation. Emollients are legitimate supportive care and a narrow cosmetic contribution, but the four-item summary of duration, distribution, primary lesion and response to occlusion is what decides whether a product or a clinician comes next.

Caveat: it is a narrative review, so the prevalence figures are pooled estimates rather than a single measured cohort.

It focuses on atopic dermatitis, so the drug options it discusses are clinical treatments and not cosmetic recommendations.

readings.note: Read the abstract and introduction for the six week definition, the histaminergic and non-histaminergic pathways, and the explicit recommendation that people over 65 presenting with pruritus should be assessed to exclude underlying malignancy. It is a short review built around a case report, so use it for the framing of assessment rather than for treatment protocols.

visual.title: Itch decision gate from duration to disposition
visual.description: A step sequence that takes a presenting itch through four questions, routes dry skin to a cosmetic plan and non-lesional chronic itch to assessment, and marks the scratch cycle as the loop that runs across both routes.
steps: Step 1, duration: mark six weeks on a horizontal timeline and label everything beyond it chronic, with the note that the threshold is a definition rather than a severity marker.
Step 2, distribution: branch into localised and generalised, and note that generalised involvement widens the differential beyond the skin.
Step 3, lesion check: branch again into a visible primary lesion and unchanged skin, and label the unchanged branch pruritus on non-lesional skin, the category most often missed.
Step 4, occlusion response: on the localised and dry branch, test a plain occlusive on damp skin for one to two weeks and mark improvement as consistent with xerosis.
Step 5, red flags: on the generalised non-lesional branch, list weight loss, fever, night sweats, jaundice, a new medicine, pregnancy and sleep disturbance, and route any of them to assessment.

Step 6, the loop: draw a circular arrow through itch, scratch, barrier damage and sensitisation, and note that it runs in both routes, so a cosmetic plan can reduce it while a clinical cause is investigated.

lessons.title: Hair loss: what a cosmetic can do, what only a clinician can diagnose
lessons.explanation: Hair is the part of the cosmetic market where the gap between what is sold and what is established is widest, and the gap closes only when a learner can name the process happening on the scalp. The hair cycle has three phases that matter. Anagen is the growth phase and lasts years; catagen is a short transition; telogen is a resting phase of roughly three months, after which the club hair is shed and a new follicle begins to grow. Shedding of something like fifty to a hundred hairs a day is normal, which is why counting hairs on a pillow without a baseline tells a learner very little. Two processes account for most of what people present with. Androgenetic alopecia is a patterned, progressive miniaturisation of genetically susceptible follicles under androgen influence, producing thinning at the temples and crown in men and a widening part with diffuse thinning over the crown in women. Telogen effluvium is a diffuse shedding of normal follicles after a trigger, and its defining feature is timing: shedding begins two to three months after the event, because the follicles that were pushed out of anagen have to pass through telogen before they are released. That lag is the single most useful piece of history in the whole topic, because it moves the search for a cause backwards by a season. The evidence base for treatment is narrower than the market suggests. A 2023 review states that only two drugs are approved by the FDA for androgenetic alopecia, topical minoxidil and oral finasteride, while noting that numerous unapproved treatments have some trial support. A 2023 Bayesian network meta-analysis pooled 17 randomised placebo-controlled trials with at least 20 participants and at least 24 weeks of follow-up, and reported terminal hair density changes at 24 weeks. In men the estimates ranged from about 10.5 to 21 hairs per square centimetre, with low-level laser comb therapy, dutasteride and a branded multi-ingredient formulation among the higher values; in women the estimates ranged from about 7 to 30 hairs per square centimetre. Three cautions belong beside those numbers. Several active treatments, including finasteride, 2 per cent minoxidil and one supplement, were not statistically separated from placebo in men. The top-ranked product was a commercial formulation, so author affiliations and funding deserve a look before the ranking is accepted. And the analysis found that responses were fastest early and then attenuated, with regrowth rates flattening or reversing after roughly 12 to 16 weeks, which means a 24-week endpoint flatters treatments that plateau. Against that background, a shampoo or a peptide serum marketed for hair growth has no mechanism for reversing miniaturisation. It may improve the cosmetic appearance of the fibre, reduce breakage, or make the scalp feel better, and those are legitimate claims, but they are not the same claim as increasing terminal hair density. The clinical boundary is drawn by the findings that a cosmetic routine cannot explain. Scarring alopecias, including lichen planopilaris and frontal fibrosing alopecia, destroy follicles permanently and often present with scalp symptoms such as itching, burning or pain, with visible inflammation, scaling or loss of the follicular openings. Alopecia areata produces sudden, well-demarcated patches, sometimes with nail changes. Trichotillomania produces irregular patches of broken hairs of different lengths. Diffuse loss accompanied by fatigue, weight change, heavy periods or other systemic symptoms points toward thyroid disease, iron deficiency or another systemic process. Rapid loss, loss in a child, or any hair loss with scalp pain, scaling or pustules belongs with a clinician, and a biopsy is sometimes required to separate a scarring from a non-scarring process. None of that can be done with a product.
lessons.example: Worked example. A 34-year-old learner reports diffuse thinning over the crown and increased shedding for six weeks. She has no scalp itching or scaling, no patches, and no family history of pattern hair loss, but she lost about eight kilograms on a restrictive diet four months ago. Work through the timeline first. Shedding began six weeks ago; the diet was four months ago. The interval is roughly the two to three months that telogen effluvium requires, which makes the diet a plausible trigger and makes the shedding a consequence rather than a new disease. Second, examine the pattern. Diffuse thinning with no frontal or temporal recession and no widening part argues against a patterned process, and the absence of scalp symptoms argues against a scarring alopecia. Third, ask what would change the conclusion: a family history, a widening part with hair diameter diversity, or shedding that continues beyond six months would each move the assessment toward androgenetic alopecia or chronic telogen effluvium. Fourth, decide the action. The appropriate plan is to correct the nutritional deficit with the help of a clinician or dietitian, maintain adequate protein and iron intake, avoid traction and harsh chemical treatments, and review at three to six months, since acute telogen effluvium remits in around 95 per cent of cases. Fifth, appraise the product she is considering, a caffeine and peptide serum with a photographic before and after. There is no randomised evidence that it reverses miniaturisation, the photographs are uncontrolled for lighting and length, and starting it now would make the eventual recovery impossible to attribute. The honest recommendation is to spend the money on the dietitian and to photograph the parting under the same light at monthly intervals instead.
lessons.question: A learner with patterned thinning at the temples wants to buy a caffeine and biotin serum, citing a trial in which a laser comb increased hair density. What is the accurate appraisal?
lessons.answer: Patterned thinning with miniaturisation suggests androgenetic alopecia, for which topical minoxidil and oral finasteride are the approved drugs, while the serum has no established mechanism for reversing miniaturisation and the laser evidence comes from pooled trials with short follow-up and commercial sponsorship to check
lessons.distractor: Because one device increased hair density in a randomised trial, light and serum treatments are interchangeable and the cheaper option is the rational choice
lessons.correction: The network meta-analysis pooled 17 randomised placebo-controlled trials of at least 20 participants and 24 weeks, and its findings are specific: terminal hair density gains of roughly 10 to 21 per square centimetre in men, several treatments not separated from placebo, and attenuation of response after 12 to 16 weeks in most arms. That is a map of the evidence, not a justification for substituting categories. Androgenetic alopecia is a diagnosis based on pattern, family history and hair diameter diversity, and a cosmetic serum does not reverse the miniaturisation that defines it. Biotin also interferes with several laboratory immunoassays, which is a reason for caution rather than enthusiasm when blood tests are being arranged.

depth.definitions: Anagen: the growth phase of the hair cycle, lasting years. Catagen: the short transitional phase. Telogen: the resting phase, roughly three months, ending in shedding. Miniaturisation: progressive reduction in hair shaft diameter and length in susceptible follicles. Androgenetic alopecia: patterned hair loss driven by androgen action on genetically susceptible follicles. Telogen effluvium: diffuse shedding of normal follicles after a trigger. Scarring alopecia: hair loss in which the follicle is destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue, with permanent loss. Hair diameter diversity: variation in shaft thickness on dermoscopy, a marker of miniaturisation. Pull test: gentle traction on a bundle of hairs to estimate the proportion in telogen. Terminal hair density: the number of thick, pigmented hairs per square centimetre.
depth.mechanism: Androgenetic alopecia is a follicular response to androgen signalling. In susceptible follicles, dihydrotestosterone shortens anagen, shrinks the dermal papilla and reduces shaft calibre, so each cycle produces a finer, shorter hair until the follicle produces only vellus hair. The process is patterned because susceptibility varies across the scalp, which is why the temples and crown are affected first. Minoxidil acts differently: it prolongs anagen and increases blood flow, probably through potassium channel opening and vascular endothelial growth factor, and its effect lasts only as long as it is used. Finasteride reduces conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which slows the miniaturisation process rather than reversing it. Telogen effluvium has no such pharmacology. A trigger pushes a proportion of follicles from anagen into catagen simultaneously, and because telogen lasts about three months, they are shed together months later. Recovery occurs when the next anagen begins, which is why the natural history is self-limiting and why any product started at the moment of shedding is credited with a recovery it did not cause.
depth.secondExample: Consider postpartum shedding. A learner gives birth and notices heavy shedding at about three to four months, with diffuse involvement and no scalp symptoms. The physiology is the same as in the diet example: pregnancy holds follicles in an extended anagen phase, and after delivery they synchronously enter catagen and telogen, producing a wave of shedding with the characteristic lag. The expected course is recovery within six to twelve months, and the appropriate management is reassurance, adequate nutrition, gentle handling and patience. Now consider the same learner at nine months if the shedding has not settled and the parting has widened with increasing hair diameter diversity. The question has changed from a self-limiting effluvium to a possible chronic process, and the next step is examination and possibly trichoscopy rather than a stronger shampoo. The teaching point is that the same symptom at two time points carries two different meanings, and the calendar is part of the evidence.
depth.mistake: The common misconception is that hair loss is a scalp cleanliness problem, so that buildup, poor washing or the wrong shampoo is the cause and a clarifying or stimulating product is the cure. There is no mechanism by which shampoo residue destroys follicles, and the belief delays the two diagnoses that matter. A second error is to attribute recovery to whatever was started at the moment shedding was noticed, when the natural history of telogen effluvium guarantees recovery in most cases. A third is to accept a before and after photograph as evidence, when lighting, hair length, styling and camera position all change the appearance more than a modest density change does. The diagnostic correction is to establish four facts before buying anything: the pattern, the duration, the presence of scalp symptoms and the timing of any possible trigger three months earlier.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take two photographs of your parting and hairline in the same place, under the same light, with the same hair length, and note the date. Then record for four weeks the number of hairs on the pillow and in the shower on wash days, the pattern of any thinning, and any scalp symptom. Finish with two sentences: the trigger that occurred two to three months before any change, and the finding that would make you seek assessment. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong record standardises the photographs, distinguishes diffuse from patterned loss, and recognises that a negative finding such as the absence of itching is informative. An entry that attributes improvement or worsening to a product started at the same time as the observation does not meet the standard.
depth.summary: Androgenetic alopecia is patterned miniaturisation with two approved drugs, minoxidil and finasteride, and a trial base whose pooled density gains are modest and whose responses attenuate after 12 to 16 weeks. Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding two to three months after a trigger, self-limiting in about 95 per cent of acute cases. A shampoo or serum can improve the appearance of fibre but has no mechanism for reversing miniaturisation. Pattern, duration, scalp symptoms and the timing of a trigger are the four facts that decide whether the next step is a product, patience, or a clinician.

visual.title: Hair cycle timeline with two diagnostic branches
visual.description: A step sequence that draws the cycle on a calendar, places the two common presentations on it, and marks the findings that route a learner to a clinician rather than a product.
steps: Step 1, cycle: draw anagen as a long band of two to six years, catagen as a narrow segment, and telogen as a band of about three months ending in shedding.
Step 2, trigger marker: place a vertical line at the trigger and a second line two to three months later, labelled shedding begins, to show why the history must be taken backwards.
Step 3, branch one: label diffuse shedding with no scalp symptoms and no pattern as telogen effluvium, and write the expected recovery and the review point at three to six months.
Step 4, branch two: label patterned thinning with hair diameter diversity as androgenetic alopecia, and attach the two approved drugs with their mechanisms.

Step 5, product boundary: draw a box labelled cosmetic effects, containing fibre appearance, breakage and scalp feel, and a separate box labelled terminal hair density, which the cosmetic cannot reach.

Step 6, referral gate: list scarring features such as pain, scaling, pustules and loss of follicular openings, sudden patches, loss in a child and rapid loss, and route all of them past the product shelf to a clinician.

lessons.title: Melasma: the clinical entity behind the cosmetic complaint
lessons.explanation: Melasma is the condition that most often sends a learner into the brightening aisle, and it is the condition least suited to being managed there. It is an acquired pigmentation disorder of sun-exposed skin, typically symmetrical, with an emphasis on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip and chin, and it is far more common in women and in people with darker skin phototypes. The reason a cosmetic serum rarely changes it is that the driver is not a single overactive enzyme but a chronic photobiological and hormonal process. Ultraviolet radiation generates reactive oxygen species, which activate signalling that increases melanocyte activity and melanin transfer; visible light does the same through a distinct route involving opsin 3, which is why a sunscreen that covers only ultraviolet can leave the pigmentation progressing; and heat, hormonal change, barrier dysfunction, mast cells and increased vascularity all contribute. That multicomponent picture predicts what the evidence shows. In a randomised comparison of 68 patients with melasma, a sunscreen covering ultraviolet and visible light produced greater improvement in a melasma severity score at eight weeks than an ultraviolet-only sunscreen, which makes photoprotection the intervention with the clearest and least contested rationale. In the topical literature, a 4 per cent hydroquinone cream produced complete clinical response in 38 per cent of patients against 8 per cent with placebo, which establishes hydroquinone as a benchmark and also shows that most patients did not achieve complete clearance. The prescription combinations used in practice, including hydroquinone with a retinoid and a corticosteroid, and oral tranexamic acid in selected patients, require diagnosis, supervision and monitoring for adverse effects, and tranexamic acid in particular requires an assessment of thrombotic risk. The legal status of the main agent is the clearest illustration of the boundary this lesson draws. Hydroquinone is not permitted as a cosmetic ingredient in the European Union, and in the United States it is a drug, available over the counter at 2 per cent and by prescription at higher strengths. A cosmetic product therefore cannot lawfully contain the benchmark ingredient, which means a brightening serum is working, if at all, through weaker mechanisms, and the learner's expectation should be set accordingly. There is also a specific harm from unmonitored use: prolonged hydroquinone without supervision is associated with exogenous ochronosis, a paradoxical blue-black pigmentation that is difficult to treat and more common in darker skin. The clinical boundary has three parts. First, diagnosis: melasma is distinguished from post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, lentigines, Hori's naevus, drug-induced pigmentation and photoallergic reactions by history and examination, and dermoscopy or Wood's lamp examination can help characterise the pattern. Second, the trigger: pregnancy, combined hormonal contraception and thyroid disease are relevant, and a clinician can review them. Third, the asymmetry of expectation: melasma is chronic and relapsing, treatment takes months, and the most reliable intervention is the one that prevents the next episode rather than the one that fades the current one. None of this makes cosmetic products useless. A well-formulated tinted sunscreen with iron oxides is doing more for a learner with melasma than most serums, and it is a cosmetic product. The distinction is between a product that reduces the driver and a product that promises to reverse the result.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner developed symmetrical brown patches on both cheeks during pregnancy and they have not faded two years later. She has used a cosmetic niacinamide serum for twelve weeks with no change and is considering a 4 per cent hydroquinone cream bought online. Work through the decisions in order. Step one, classify. Symmetrical, photodistributed, pregnancy-associated pigmentation in a woman of reproductive age is the classic presentation of melasma, and the history of persistence after delivery fits the chronic relapsing course. Step two, check the product she used. Niacinamide is a legitimate cosmetic ingredient with modest evidence for pigment, but it acts on melanosome transfer rather than on the photobiological driver, and twelve weeks is at the short end of the interval over which any pigment change is measurable. A null result is therefore uninformative about the condition and mildly informative about the product. Step three, examine the online purchase. A 4 per cent hydroquinone product bought without a prescription is either an unregulated import or a mislabelled cosmetic, and in either case the learner cannot verify the concentration, the stability or the presence of a corticosteroid, which is a common undocumented addition in products sold for rapid lightening. Step four, rank the interventions by evidence and risk. Photoprotection with a tinted, iron-oxide-containing sunscreen every day has the clearest rationale and the lowest risk. Diagnosis by a clinician establishes the pattern, reviews hormonal contributors and excludes mimics. Prescription treatment, if offered, comes with monitoring for irritation and ochronosis. Step five, set the expectation in numbers. A benchmark topical achieved complete clearance in 38 per cent of patients against 8 per cent on placebo, so even the best single agent leaves most people improved rather than clear, and relapse after stopping is the norm. A learner who understands that will judge the plan by control over months rather than by disappearance over weeks.
lessons.question: A learner with symmetrical cheek pigmentation since pregnancy has used a cosmetic brightening serum for three months without change, and asks whether to buy a 4 per cent hydroquinone cream online. What is the correct appraisal?
lessons.answer: The pattern is consistent with melasma, which needs diagnosis and photoprotection including visible light, and hydroquinone at 4 per cent is a prescription-strength drug in the United States and not permitted in cosmetics in the European Union, so an unregulated online purchase carries concentration, stability and adulteration risks
lessons.distractor: The cosmetic serum failed because the concentration was too low, so a 4 per cent hydroquinone cream from an online seller is the logical next step and will work faster
lessons.correction: Melasma is a chronic photobiological and hormonal disorder rather than a single overactive enzyme, and its management is ranked by the driver. A randomised comparison of 68 patients found that a sunscreen covering ultraviolet and visible light produced greater improvement in a melasma severity score at eight weeks than an ultraviolet-only product, which is the strongest and safest intervention available. A 4 per cent hydroquinone cream produced complete response in 38 per cent of patients against 8 per cent with placebo, which establishes both its status as a benchmark and the modest ceiling of a single agent. Because 4 per cent hydroquinone is a prescription medicine in the United States and is not permitted in cosmetics in Europe, an online purchase cannot be verified for concentration or for undeclared corticosteroids, and prolonged unsupervised use carries a risk of exogenous ochronosis.

depth.definitions: Melasma: an acquired, symmetrical, photodistributed pigmentation disorder, most common on the face in women and in darker skin phototypes. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation: pigment deposited after inflammation or injury at the site of that injury. Melanocyte: the cell that produces melanin within melanosomes. Tyrosinase: the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis. Hydroquinone: a tyrosinase inhibitor used as a depigmenting drug. Exogenous ochronosis: a paradoxical blue-black pigmentation associated with prolonged hydroquinone use. Triple combination: a prescription formulation combining hydroquinone, a retinoid and a corticosteroid. Tranexamic acid: an antifibrinolytic drug used orally and topically in melasma, with thrombotic risk requiring assessment. Melasma area and severity score: a clinical index used to grade extent and intensity. Opsin 3: a photoreceptor in melanocytes implicated in visible light induced pigmentation.
depth.mechanism: Pigment is produced when ultraviolet or visible radiation, hormones or inflammatory mediators increase tyrosinase activity and melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes. In melasma the melanocytes are not simply overactive; the dermis contains melanophages, the basement membrane is often disrupted, mast cell numbers are increased and the vasculature is more prominent, which is why the pigmentation can persist after the epidermis turns over and why treatments aimed only at tyrosinase produce partial results. Visible light matters because it penetrates to the dermis and activates opsin 3 in melanocytes, producing pigmentation that lasts longer than the ultraviolet response, and because conventional sunscreens transmit most of that waveband. Iron oxides in tinted formulations attenuate visible light by scattering and absorption, which is the physical basis for using them. Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase and alters melanosome structure, producing a dose-dependent reduction in pigmentation; its association with ochronosis is linked to cumulative exposure without monitoring, and the risk is higher in darker skin, which is also the population in which melasma is most common.
depth.secondExample: Consider a learner with a single dark mark on the cheek at the site of a healed spot, and compare the management. The history is the discriminator: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows a recognisable injury at the same site, is usually solitary or scattered rather than symmetrical, and fades as epidermal turnover proceeds, although it can take many months in darker skin. The driver was inflammation, not light and hormones, so the intervention is to stop the inflammation and protect the site, not to suppress tyrosinase aggressively. Applying a prescription-strength depigmenting agent to a resolving mark adds irritation and, in darker skin, can produce the pigment it was meant to treat. Now consider a third pattern: small, sharply defined brown macules on the cheeks in an older person, which are lentigines and behave differently again, being amenable to different treatments and not driven by hormones. Three patterns, three plans, and the diagnostic step precedes the product in every case.
depth.mistake: The error is to treat every dark patch as one condition and every brightening product as one mechanism, so that a serum failing once means a stronger product is needed. Melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and lentigines differ in driver, distribution and natural history, and only one of them is chronic and relapsing. A second error is to assume that a product bought online at a stated percentage contains that percentage, when unregulated imports are the specific category in which concentration, stability and undeclared corticosteroids cannot be assumed. The diagnostic correction is to ask three questions: is the pigmentation symmetrical and photodistributed, did it follow an injury at the same site, and is the pattern stable, fluctuating or seasonal. The answers place the learner in a category before any ingredient is discussed.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Photograph your pigmentation in standard light, record the distribution and symmetry on a simple face diagram, note the date of onset and any hormonal or inflammatory trigger, and list every product currently used on the area. Then write two sentences: the photoprotection step you will change first, and the question you would put to a clinician. Standard for a complete record: a strong record distinguishes symmetrical from localised pigmentation, notices whether the product contains a tint or iron oxides, and does not claim a diagnosis. It should recognise that a cosmetic trial of twelve weeks cannot settle a question about a chronic relapsing condition. An entry that lists products without describing the pattern does not yet meet the standard.
depth.summary: Melasma is a chronic, symmetrical, photodistributed pigmentation disorder driven by ultraviolet and visible light, hormones and a dermal inflammatory and vascular component. Photoprotection that covers visible light produced greater improvement than ultraviolet-only protection in a randomised comparison of 68 patients, hydroquinone 4 per cent produced complete response in 38 per cent against 8 per cent with placebo, and the prescription combinations and oral tranexamic acid that follow require diagnosis and monitoring. Hydroquinone is a drug, not a cosmetic ingredient in the European Union, and unregulated online purchases carry unverifiable concentration and adulteration risk. Diagnosis, trigger review and expectation setting come before any product.

visual.title: Pigment decision tree with a legal boundary
visual.description: A step sequence that separates melasma from its mimics on history and distribution, attaches the driver to the intervention, and draws the line between cosmetic and prescription agents.
steps: Step 1, distribution: draw a face diagram and mark symmetrical cheek, forehead and upper lip involvement on one side, and a single localised mark at a site of injury on the other.

Step 2, history: under the symmetrical branch write pregnancy, hormonal contraception, thyroid disease and years of sun exposure; under the localised branch write the preceding spot, burn or procedure.
Step 3, driver: label the symmetrical branch ultraviolet, visible light and hormones, and the localised branch inflammation with post-inflammatory pigment deposition.
Step 4, intervention: attach daily tinted sunscreen with iron oxides to the first branch, and stopping the inflammation plus time and protection to the second.

Step 5, legal boundary: draw a vertical line across the diagram and place cosmetic agents such as niacinamide and azelaic acid on one side, and hydroquinone, retinoids, corticosteroids and oral tranexamic acid on the other, labelled prescription.
Step 6, expectation: write the benchmark numbers beside the prescription side, 38 per cent complete response against 8 per cent with placebo, and note that relapse after stopping is usual.

lessons.title: Photosensitivity: when light plus a substance, or light alone, produces a rash
lessons.explanation: A rash that appears on sun-exposed skin after a sunny weekend usually has one of three explanations, and they are managed differently. The first is an exaggerated sunburn, which is a dose problem in normal skin. The second is a phototoxic reaction, in which a chemical in the skin absorbs radiation and generates reactive species that damage tissue directly. The third is a photoallergic reaction, in which radiation converts a chemical into an antigen and the immune system mounts a delayed response. The distinction between the last two is practical rather than academic. Phototoxicity can occur in anyone who takes enough of the drug and receives enough light; it appears within hours, looks like a burn or an exaggerated sunburn confined to exposed skin, and is dose dependent. Photoallergy occurs only in people who have been sensitised; it is eczematous, may spread beyond exposed areas, and can persist after the exposure stops. The range of culprit substances is larger than most learners expect. A 2021 review of drug-induced photosensitivity tabulates the reported agents by class, and the counts show where the exposure sits: 70 anti-infectives, including 16 fluoroquinolones and 7 tetracyclines; 60 cardiovascular drugs, including thiazide diuretics and amiodarone; 38 anti-inflammatory drugs, of which 28 are non-steroidal agents; and 47 antineoplastic drugs. Several of those classes are prescribed to people who also use cosmetics, and some, such as the tetracyclines, are prescribed for acne itself, which is how a learner with acne ends up with a burning face after a walk. Fragrances, sunscreen filters, plants and topical agents add further routes, and phytophotodermatitis from lime, celery, fig or giant hogweed produces streaky pigmentation that is often mistaken for an allergic reaction. The other major category is idiopathic, and polymorphic light eruption is the most common of these. It affects an estimated 11 to 21 per cent of people in temperate climates, is more common further from the equator, and presents as itchy red papules, vesicles or plaques on exposed skin within hours of exposure, healing without scarring within about 14 days. It characteristically begins in spring, fades by autumn and recurs the following year, and the twin data are striking: concordance of about 0.72 in monozygotic pairs against 0.30 in dizygotic pairs, with segregation analysis suggesting that a majority of the population carries a low-penetrance susceptibility allele. The mechanism is understood as a failure of the normal ultraviolet-induced immunosuppression that usually follows exposure, so the skin mounts a delayed hypersensitivity response to antigens generated by the light itself. The cosmetic implications are narrower than the marketing suggests. A sunscreen reduces the radiation dose and is a sensible adjunct, but it does not prevent a phototoxic reaction in someone taking a sufficient dose of a culprit drug, and it cannot substitute for reviewing the drug. Clothing, shade, timing and attention to reflected light from water, sand and snow reduce exposure more reliably than a higher SPF. For polymorphic light eruption, the recognised measures are photoprotection, short courses of topical corticosteroids for flares, and hardening through gradual exposure or phototherapy, all of which are clinical decisions. It is worth stating plainly that the Cochrane review intended to assess interventions for this condition exists only as a published protocol, so the formal evidence base for specific treatments is weaker than the number of available options implies. The safety rule follows. A learner should not stop a prescribed medicine because of a photosensitive reaction, because the consequences of stopping can exceed the skin problem, and amiodarone in particular persists in tissue for a long time after any change. The correct action is to keep the skin protected, document the timing and distribution, and bring the medication list to the prescriber.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner taking doxycycline for acne spends an afternoon gardening in strong spring sun and develops sharply defined redness and burning on the forearms, the V of the neck and the face by that evening, sparing the areas covered by her shirt. She asks which sunscreen to switch to. Step one, characterise the pattern. The distribution corresponds exactly to exposed skin with sharp borders, the onset is within hours, the sensation is burning rather than itching, and there is no eczematous spread. That combination is phototoxic rather than photoallergic. Step two, identify the chromophore. Tetracyclines are among the anti-infective classes enumerated in the drug photosensitivity literature, and the timing relative to starting the antibiotic is the relevant history. Step three, decide what sunscreen can and cannot do. It reduces the radiation reaching the skin, and it is worth using, but the reaction is driven by the combination of drug concentration in the skin and light dose, so a higher SPF reduces the probability and severity without abolishing the risk. Step four, act on the right variable. The learner should contact the prescriber to discuss whether the drug can be changed, whether the dose can be adjusted, and what alternatives exist for her acne, and she should not stop it herself. Meanwhile, clothing with a tight weave, a wide brim, shade between the peak hours and avoidance of reflective surfaces do more than a product swap. Step five, contrast with photoallergy. If instead she had developed an itchy, eczematous rash on the neck and the backs of the hands two days after applying a new fragrance, with spread beyond the exposed area, the pattern would suggest photoallergy, and the relevant investigation would be photopatch testing rather than a drug review. Same sun, different mechanism, different next step.
lessons.question: A learner on a prescribed antibiotic develops a burning, sharply bordered redness on the forearms and face after gardening, and asks which sunscreen will prevent it recurring. What is the correct response?
lessons.answer: This is a phototoxic pattern that sunscreen cannot reliably prevent on its own, so she should contact the prescriber about the drug while using clothing and shade, and she should not stop the medicine herself
lessons.distractor: The reaction shows the sunscreen was inadequate, so a higher SPF with a mineral filter will prevent recurrence and the antibiotic can continue unchanged
lessons.correction: Phototoxicity is a direct, dose-related injury produced when a drug chromophore absorbs radiation and generates reactive species; it can occur in anyone with sufficient drug and light, appears within hours and is confined to exposed skin. Tetracyclines are among the 70 anti-infective agents enumerated in the drug photosensitivity literature, which also lists 60 cardiovascular and 38 anti-inflammatory agents. Sunscreen lowers the radiation dose and is worth using, but it does not abolish a reaction driven by drug concentration in tissue, and the decision to continue, change or stop a prescribed drug belongs to the prescriber. Stopping an antibiotic for acne unsupervised risks treatment failure and contributes to resistance.

depth.definitions: Phototoxicity: direct, dose-related tissue injury from a chemical activated by radiation. Photoallergy: a delayed immune reaction to an antigen formed when radiation alters a chemical in the skin. Action spectrum: the range of wavelengths that produce a given effect. Photopatch test: a procedure in which substances are applied and then irradiated to identify photoallergic sensitisers. Phytophotodermatitis: a reaction produced by plant chemicals, typically furocoumarins, plus ultraviolet exposure. Polymorphic light eruption: an idiopathic, recurrent, itchy eruption on exposed skin after sun exposure. Hardening: the reduction in reactivity achieved by gradually increasing exposure. Ultraviolet index: an international scale of erythemally effective solar radiation.
depth.mechanism: A photosensitiser works by absorbing a photon and entering an excited state. In phototoxicity the excited molecule transfers energy to oxygen, producing singlet oxygen and other reactive species that damage membranes, proteins and DNA, which is why the reaction looks like a burn and is proportional to dose. In photoallergy the excited molecule or its metabolite binds to proteins, creating an antigen that triggers a T cell response on re-exposure, which is why the rash is eczematous, delayed and not strictly proportional to dose. The action spectrum is usually long-wave ultraviolet, because those wavelengths penetrate further and because many drug chromophores absorb in that region. Amiodarone is an extreme example: it is highly lipophilic with a long elimination half-life, so the skin burden persists for weeks to months after the drug is stopped, which is a pharmacokinetic reason why stopping is not an instant fix. Polymorphic light eruption is different again, involving a failure of ultraviolet-induced immunosuppression so that the skin reacts to antigens generated by exposure itself.
depth.secondExample: Consider a learner who returns from a holiday with streaky, linear brown marks on the forearms and the side of the neck, and who assumes she has developed an allergy to her sunscreen. The distribution follows the tracks of a plant, the pigmentation appears days after the exposure and the itch, if present, was mild and transient. That is phytophotodermatitis: furocoumarins from lime, celery, fig or giant hogweed deposited on skin, followed by sunlight, producing a phototoxic reaction whose pigment can persist for months. No allergy has been demonstrated and no product needs to be avoided, although sun protection while the pigment settles is sensible. Contrast this with a learner who develops an itchy eczematous rash on the face and neck each time she uses a particular sunscreen, with spread beyond the application site and a delay of a day or two. That pattern suggests photoallergy to a filter, and the appropriate step is photopatch testing rather than repeated product trials. Two rashes after sun, two mechanisms, and the difference is visible in the shape and the timing.
depth.mistake: The common error is to treat every reaction to sun as an allergy to a product, which leads to repeated product swaps and misses the drug, the plant or the idiopathic condition. The opposite error is to treat a photosensitive reaction as sunburn and to conclude that the learner simply needs a higher SPF, when the dose-response relationship means that no practical SPF abolishes a phototoxic reaction. A third error is to stop a prescribed medicine without advice, particularly a cardiac or antimicrobial drug, which can produce harm larger than the skin problem. The diagnostic correction is a four-part description: the shape of the rash, the timing relative to exposure, the drugs and plants involved, and whether the rash spread beyond exposed skin. Those four items separate the three mechanisms before any product is chosen.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. List every medicine you take, including over-the-counter and topical products, with the date each was started, and mark any that appear in a drug photosensitivity list. Then record one week of sun exposure with the time of day, the duration, the clothing worn and any reaction. Finish with one sentence for the prescriber and one sentence describing the protection plan you will use meanwhile. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong record includes start dates, notices that a reaction beginning weeks after a new drug is still temporally plausible, and recognises that clothing and timing do more than a higher SPF. An entry that names only the sunscreen does not yet meet the standard.
depth.summary: Photosensitivity has three common mechanisms: phototoxicity, which is direct and dose related and occurs in anyone with enough drug and light; photoallergy, which is immune, delayed and eczematous; and idiopathic conditions such as polymorphic light eruption, which affects an estimated 11 to 21 per cent of people in temperate climates and reflects a failure of ultraviolet-induced immunosuppression. The culprit drug list is broad, with 70 anti-infectives, 60 cardiovascular agents, 38 anti-inflammatory agents and 47 antineoplastic agents tabulated in one review. Sunscreen is an adjunct rather than a solution, clothing and timing are more reliable, and the decision about a prescribed drug belongs to the prescriber.
