visual.title: Three mechanisms branching from one exposed rash
visual.description: A step sequence that takes a rash in a sun-exposed distribution and separates sunburn, phototoxicity and photoallergy by shape, timing and dose relationship, then adds the idiopathic branch.
steps: Step 1, distribution: shade the areas that were exposed and leave the covered areas clear, noting that a sharp border following clothing is the first clue.
Step 2, timing: place onset within hours on one arm of the diagram and onset after one to two days on the other, since immediate burning and delayed eczema point different ways.
Step 3, morphology: label the immediate branch as burn-like or exaggerated sunburn, and the delayed branch as itchy, eczematous and possibly spreading beyond exposed skin.
Step 4, dose relationship: annotate the burn-like branch as proportional to drug and light dose and possible in anyone, and the eczematous branch as occurring only after sensitisation.
Step 5, exposure list: attach the drug classes with their counts, 70 anti-infectives, 60 cardiovascular, 38 anti-inflammatory, 47 antineoplastic, plus plants, fragrances and filters.

Step 6, idiopathic branch: add a separate route labelled recurrent spring eruption healing within 14 days, and mark it as a clinical diagnosis with photoprotection, topical treatment for flares and hardening as the recognised measures.

lessons.title: Capstone: an n-of-1 test you can defend, and a handoff note that carries the evidence
lessons.explanation: Every earlier level asked whether a product works. This lesson asks the harder and more useful question: whether it works for one person, and what would count as knowing. The design that answers it is the n-of-1 trial, a randomised crossover study conducted in a single individual, in which periods of active product and control alternate in a random order and the outcome is measured the same way in every period. The 2015 CONSORT extension for reporting n-of-1 trials exists because these studies were being reported so inconsistently that readers could not tell a real effect from an artefact. A 2024 methodological review of randomised n-of-1 trials published between 2011 and 2023 identified 74 studies, of which 13 were in rare conditions, with a median of 9 participants and interquartile range of 4 to 20, and 12 trials involving a single patient. That distribution tells a learner something important: the design is used both for formal research and for individual clinical decisions, and the same reporting standards apply to both. The components are the ones lesson 63 taught, applied within one person. Randomisation of the order of periods protects against the expectation that the first period will be better. Blinding, where possible, protects against differential judgement. Washout protects against carryover, the persistence of an effect from one period into the next. A pre-specified outcome and a pre-specified decision rule protect against the most common human error, which is looking at the data and then deciding what would count as success. The arithmetic is unforgiving, which is why most self-tests are underpowered. Suppose a learner scores texture from zero to ten each day and completes four pairs of two-week periods. The relevant variability is not the day-to-day spread but the spread of the period-level difference, and even if that is as low as 1.2 points, the standard error of the mean difference with four pairs is 1.2 divided by the square root of four, which is 0.6. A 95 per cent interval around an observed difference of 0.8 points then runs from roughly minus 1.1 to plus 2.7, because with three degrees of freedom the multiplier is about 3.2. The interval includes zero and also includes differences large enough to matter, so the honest conclusion is that the test detected nothing, not that the product does nothing. Two further design facts follow. Carryover is the threat that matters most for cosmetics, because retinoids and acids change epidermal turnover over weeks, so a one-week washout can leave activity in the control periods and shrink the observed difference. Period effects are the second, because season, humidity, sun exposure and the state of the barrier all drift across a month, and randomising the order protects against a systematic drift only partly. The capstone deliverable is therefore not a verdict. It is a record: what was tested, at what concentration, on which site, for how long, with what measured outcome, what was observed, what went wrong, and what question remains. That record is what makes a clinical conversation efficient, and it is the same discipline lesson 70 applied to a product dossier. Where the question is clinical, the record is what a clinician needs in order to help rather than to start from the beginning.
lessons.example: Worked example with arithmetic. A learner wants to know whether a 0.05 per cent tretinoin cream improves the texture of her right cheek compared with her usual moisturiser. She designs four pairs of two-week periods, alternating active and control in a random order, with a one-week washout between periods. Her outcome is a texture score from zero to ten, recorded daily and averaged per period, and she asks a friend to photograph the cheek under the same lamp on the last day of each period without knowing which product was in use. Step one, check the arithmetic before running it. She has four paired differences. If the standard deviation of the period-level difference is 1.2 points, the standard error of the mean difference is 0.6, and the 95 per cent interval around an observed mean difference multiplies that by about 3.18, giving plus or minus 1.9 points. To detect a difference of 1 point reliably, she would need a much larger number of pairs or a much less variable outcome. Step two, examine the carryover assumption. Tretinoin alters epidermal turnover and barrier function over weeks, so a one-week washout is shorter than the effect it is meant to clear, and the control periods will not be clean. That biases the comparison toward zero. Step three, examine the period effect. Four periods span roughly eleven weeks including washouts, which crosses a seasonal change in humidity in many climates, so the later periods are not exchangeable with the earlier ones. Step four, interpret a result honestly. If the mean difference is 0.8 points with an interval from minus 1.1 to plus 2.7, the correct statement is that no difference was detected, and the decision should be made on tolerance, cost and the absence of irritation rather than on a claimed benefit. If instead the difference were 3 points with the same variability, the interval would exclude zero and the conclusion would be that a difference was detected in this person over this period, which is still not a claim about anyone else. Step five, write the record. Product, concentration, vehicle, site, dose, period length, washout, randomisation method, blinding arrangement, outcome definition, result with its interval, adverse events, and the question that remains. That paragraph is the deliverable, and it is more valuable than the verdict.
lessons.question: A learner tests a new serum on one cheek for four two-week periods, alternating with her usual moisturiser, with a one-week washout. The mean difference in her texture score is 0.8 points and the 95 per cent interval runs from minus 1.1 to 2.7. What is the correct conclusion?
lessons.answer: No difference was detected: the interval includes zero and also includes differences large enough to matter, so the test is inconclusive rather than negative, and the decision should rest on tolerance, cost and adverse effects
lessons.distractor: The serum produced a measurable improvement of 0.8 points, so it should be continued and the result recorded as evidence that the product works
lessons.correction: An estimate without its interval is not a result. With four paired periods and a period-level standard deviation of about 1.2 points, the standard error of the mean difference is 0.6 and the 95 per cent interval spans roughly plus or minus 1.9 points, so an observed 0.8 is compatible with no effect and with a clinically useful effect. The design also has two specific weaknesses that bias toward zero: a one-week washout is shorter than the persistence of a retinoid or acid effect, and four periods spanning about eleven weeks cross seasonal and humidity change. The honest entry in the record is that the test could not distinguish the products, which is different from evidence that they are equivalent.

depth.definitions: N-of-1 trial: a randomised, multi-period crossover study conducted in a single person. Period: a defined interval during which one treatment is used. Washout: a gap between periods intended to let the previous treatment's effect dissipate. Carryover: persistence of an effect from one period into the next. Period effect: a change over time that affects all treatments, such as season or disease drift. Blinding: withholding knowledge of the allocated treatment from the participant, the assessor or both. Pre-specification: writing the outcome and the decision rule before data collection. Standard error of the mean difference: the standard deviation of the paired differences divided by the square root of the number of pairs. Minimal clinically important difference: the smallest change a person would regard as worthwhile. CENT: the CONSORT extension for reporting n-of-1 trials.
depth.mechanism: A crossover design is efficient because each person serves as their own control, so between-person variability drops out of the comparison. That efficiency is bought with an assumption: the effect of one period must not persist into the next, and the periods must be otherwise comparable. Cosmetics violate both assumptions in predictable ways. Structural agents change the epidermis over weeks, so their effect outlasts a short washout and contaminates the control periods, which reduces the observed difference rather than inflating it. Seasonal and humidity change shifts baseline barrier function across a month, so later periods are not exchangeable with earlier ones, and randomising the order only converts a systematic trend into noise. Subjective outcomes add a judgement channel that blinding closes, which is why an assessor who does not know the schedule is worth more than a more precise scale. Underneath all of this sits sampling error: with four pairs, the interval around the estimate is wide, and a wide interval cannot support a claim either way.
depth.secondExample: Consider a different question with the same machinery: which of two sunscreens a learner actually wears. The outcome is not efficacy but adherence, measured as the number of days per fortnight the product was used, which is countable and does not require a scale. The design still alternates periods, but blinding is impossible because the products look different, so the learner substitutes an objective measure for a blinded one. Here the n-of-1 logic produces a clean answer, because the effect size is large and the measurement is unambiguous: if one product is used on twelve days and the other on three, the comparison does not need an interval to be persuasive. The contrast with the tretinoin example is the lesson. A design is not strong or weak in the abstract; it is adequate or inadequate for a particular effect size and a particular outcome. Choosing an outcome with low measurement error, such as days used or lesion count, is often more valuable than adding periods.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is the informal before and after: a photograph in different light, a judgement after nine days, two changes at once, and a conclusion that the product worked. The second error is the opposite, treating a null self-test as proof of no effect, when the design could only have detected a large difference. The third is to generalise a personal result into a claim about other people, which the single-person design cannot support. The diagnostic correction is to write four items before starting: the outcome and how it is measured, the number of pairs and the washout justified by the product's known persistence, the blinding arrangement, and the decision rule including what result would count as inconclusive. If those four cannot be written, the test will produce an opinion rather than a finding.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Write a one-page protocol for testing one product, containing the question, the product and concentration, the site, the period length and washout, the randomisation method, the outcome and its scale, the assessor and their blinding, the decision rule, and the stop rule for irritation. Then write the handoff note you would give a clinician: what was tried, for how long, what happened, what else changed, and the specific question you want answered. Rubric: a strong protocol justifies the washout by the product's mechanism, states the arithmetic limit of the number of pairs chosen, and separates a detected difference from a clinically useful one. A strong note is factual, dated and free of conclusions the design cannot support. A protocol that names only the product and the duration does not yet meet the standard.
depth.summary: An n-of-1 trial is a randomised multi-period crossover in one person, and its quality depends on the same components as any trial: randomisation of order, blinding of assessment, a washout matched to the product's persistence, a pre-specified outcome and a pre-specified decision rule. With four pairs the interval around an observed difference is wide enough that most cosmetic effects cannot be distinguished, and carryover and seasonal drift both bias toward finding nothing. The deliverable is a dated record with the result and its uncertainty, which is also the most useful thing to bring to a clinician, because it converts a vague complaint into a specific question.

readings.title: A methodological review of randomised n-of-1 trials (2024, Trials, PMC)
readings.note: Read the abstract and methods for the search period, the 74 included trials, the 13 in rare conditions, the median of 9 participants with an interquartile range of 4 to 20, and the 12 single-patient trials. Then read the results for how often washout, blinding and randomisation were reported, which is the practical gap this lesson addresses.

readings.title: The development of a set of key points to aid clinicians and researchers in designing and conducting n-of-1 trials (2024, Trials, PMC)
readings.note: Read the key points list for the design decisions a defensible n-of-1 trial requires, particularly the justification of period length, washout and the analysis plan. It is a consensus and methods paper rather than a trial, so use it as a checklist, and note that its focus is clinical rather than cosmetic use.

readings.title: CONSORT extension for reporting N-of-1 trials (CENT) 2015 Statement (PubMed record)
readings.note: Read the record and the abstract for the scope of the reporting guideline, namely what a published n-of-1 trial must disclose about design, allocation, blinding and analysis. The full statement was published in the BMJ and the record here may not include the complete text, so use it to identify the reporting items rather than as a substitute for the checklist itself.

visual.title: Four-period n-of-1 schedule with a washout and a decision gate
visual.description: A step sequence that lays the alternating periods on a timeline, marks where carryover and seasonal drift enter, and places the interval arithmetic and the decision rule at the end.
steps: Step 1, timeline: draw four two-week periods as alternating blocks labelled active and control in a randomly chosen order, with a one-week washout between each pair.
Step 2, carryover: shade the first days of each period and label them residual activity, noting that the shading should be wider for retinoids and acids than for a simple moisturiser.

Step 3, period effect: draw a rising or falling trend line across the whole timeline and label it season, humidity and barrier drift, then note that randomisation converts it into noise rather than removing it.
Step 4, measurement: attach the outcome to each period, with the instrument or scale, the assessor and whether the assessor is blinded to the schedule.
Step 5, arithmetic: write the observed mean difference, the standard deviation of the paired differences, the number of pairs and the resulting interval, and mark whether the interval crosses zero.
Step 6, decision gate: place two exits, one labelled detected and worth continuing, one labelled inconclusive and decided on tolerance and cost, and forbid a third exit labelled proven ineffective.

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old learner reports generalised itching for three months, worse at night, with no visible rash. She has tried three 'soothing' body lotions and an oat-based cream. What is the correct response?
questions.answer: Generalised itch lasting more than six weeks on apparently unchanged skin is a recognised clinical category with systemic causes, so she needs assessment including blood tests, and emollients are supportive care rather than a diagnostic trial
questions.distractor: Itch without a rash is dry skin by definition, so the answer is a thicker occlusive applied twice daily for eight weeks before considering anything else
questions.correction: Chronic pruritus on primarily non-lesional skin is its own category in the International Forum for the Study of Itch classification, precisely because it often has no primary skin disease. Prevalence estimates run from 8 to 25 per cent, rising to about 25 per cent in people aged 65 and over, and the differential includes cholestasis, chronic kidney disease, haematological disease, thyroid dysfunction and medication effects. Nocturnal generalised itch in an older person is a pattern that warrants examination and laboratory testing. An emollient is reasonable comfort care, but an eight-week cosmetic trial before assessment delays a diagnosis, which is the failure mode lesson 57 described.

questions.prompt: Three months after childbirth a learner notices heavy diffuse shedding on her pillow and in the shower. She has no scalp symptoms, no patches and no family history of pattern loss, and she asks which growth serum to buy. What is the best answer?
questions.answer: The timing and diffuse pattern fit acute telogen effluvium, which usually remits on its own within six months, so the priority is correcting any trigger and waiting rather than buying a growth product
questions.distractor: Postpartum hair loss is permanent unless treated early, so a caffeine and peptide serum should be started immediately to prevent follicle loss
questions.correction: Acute telogen effluvium is defined as shedding lasting under six months, typically beginning two to three months after a trigger such as childbirth, fever, surgery, haemorrhage or rapid weight loss, and it remits in around 95 per cent of cases. The three-month lag is the giveaway: the shedding reflects follicles that left the growth phase months earlier, which is why a product started at the moment of shedding cannot be credited with the recovery. A cosmetic serum has no mechanism for reversing that cycle. The clinical questions are whether the pattern is diffuse, whether there are scalp symptoms or patches, and whether the loss continues beyond six months, because those change the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A learner developed symmetrical brown patches on both cheeks during pregnancy. Twelve weeks of a cosmetic niacinamide brightening serum have changed nothing. She asks whether to buy a stronger over-the-counter lightener. What is the correct appraisal?
questions.answer: The pattern is consistent with melasma, a clinical diagnosis in which photoprotection including visible light is the intervention with the clearest rationale, and the prescription options that follow diagnosis are not cosmetic purchases, with hydroquinone not permitted in cosmetics in the European Union
questions.distractor: The serum failed because the concentration was too low, so a higher-strength over-the-counter lightener with hydroquinone is the logical next step
questions.correction: Melasma is an acquired, symmetrical, photodistributed pigmentation disorder with a hormonal and genetic component, and it is diagnosed clinically rather than by product response. The relevant evidence is not a brighter serum but a randomised comparison of 68 patients in which a sunscreen covering ultraviolet and visible light produced greater improvement in a melasma severity score at eight weeks than a ultraviolet-only sunscreen, and a 4 per cent hydroquinone cream against placebo producing complete response in 38 per cent versus 8 per cent. Hydroquinone is a medicinal ingredient in the European Union and long unmonitored use carries a risk of exogenous ochronosis, so the step after diagnosis belongs with a prescriber.

questions.prompt: A learner taking doxycycline for acne spends an afternoon gardening and develops a sharply defined burning redness on the forearms, neck and face by evening. She wants to know which sunscreen to switch to. What is the correct response?
questions.answer: This is a phototoxic pattern that sunscreen cannot prevent on its own, so she should contact the prescriber about the drug while using clothing, shade and a broad-spectrum product as adjuncts, and she should not stop the medicine on her own
questions.distractor: The reaction shows her sunscreen failed, so a higher SPF with a physical filter will solve the problem and the antibiotic can continue unchanged
questions.correction: Phototoxicity is a direct, dose-related tissue injury produced when a drug chromophore absorbs ultraviolet or visible radiation and generates reactive species; it can occur in anyone taking enough of the drug, appears within hours and looks like an exaggerated sunburn confined to exposed skin. Tetracyclines are among the anti-infective classes enumerated in the drug photosensitivity literature, which lists 70 anti-infectives including 7 tetracyclines and 16 fluoroquinolones. Sunscreen reduces but does not abolish the exposure that drives the reaction, and the decision about continuing, substituting or adjusting the drug belongs to the prescriber. Stopping an antibiotic for acne unsupervised risks treatment failure and resistance.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to know whether a new serum reduces her cheek redness. She applies it to the left cheek only, changes her pillowcase at the same time, takes phone photos at different times of day, and decides after nine days that the left side looks better. How should this test be judged?
questions.answer: The test cannot answer the question: it changed more than one variable, ran for less than a typical biological response window, used uncontrolled photographs and had no pre-specified decision rule, so a paired multi-period design with a fixed outcome and a blinded assessor is needed
questions.distractor: Because the product was applied to one cheek only, the comparison is internally controlled and the visible improvement on that side is sufficient evidence
questions.correction: A one-sided application controls for between-person differences but not for any of the things that actually vary here: a new pillowcase, different lighting and time of day, and a judgement made after the fact with no threshold for what would count as improvement. Nine days is shorter than the interval over which barrier and pigment change is measurable. A defensible self-test specifies the outcome in advance, holds everything else constant, alternates product and control in several periods with a washout, and has someone who does not know which period is which make the assessment. Where the difference falls inside the day-to-day variation, the honest conclusion is that no difference was detected.

questions.prompt: A learner says she only buys cosmetics that are 'FDA approved'. Which statement correctly describes what United States law actually provides for a moisturiser?
questions.answer: Cosmetics are not approved before sale; since 2022 the responsible person must register facilities, list products and ingredients, report serious adverse events and hold safety substantiation records, but no pre-market authorisation is granted
questions.distractor: The FDA reviews and approves each cosmetic formulation before it can be sold, which is why products carry an approval number
questions.correction: Approval is a drug and device concept. For cosmetics the federal framework prohibits adulterated and misbranded products and, since the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022, requires facility registration, product listing, serious adverse event reporting and records supporting safety substantiation, with the agency stating that neither the law nor its regulations require specific tests. No approval number exists to check. The practical consequence is that 'FDA approved' on a cosmetic label is either a misstatement or a reference to something else, such as a facility registration.

questions.prompt: A device sold online is described as 'FDA registered' and 'clinically proven to boost collagen'. It is a 1.5 mm microneedling roller for home use. What is the accurate assessment?
questions.answer: The FDA has not authorised any microneedling medical device for over-the-counter sale, registration is a facility or listing status rather than a device clearance, and a 1.5 mm roller penetrates deeply enough to carry infection and pigment risk
questions.distractor: Registration means the device has been reviewed by the FDA, so home use at 1.5 mm is acceptable if the instructions are followed
questions.correction: The FDA consumer guidance distinguishes cleared microneedling devices, used by trained providers for facial acne scars, facial wrinkles and abdominal scars in people aged 22 and older, from short blunt rollers that claim only to exfoliate and are therefore not medical devices at all. It states that no microneedling medical device has been authorised for over-the-counter sale. 'Registered' can refer to a facility registration or a listing, neither of which is a clearance, and depth determines both effect and risk: penetration to 1.5 mm reaches the dermis, where contamination and trauma produce infection, granulomas and pigment change.

questions.prompt: A learner compares a European sunscreen labelled SPF 50+ with a United States product labelled SPF 100 and assumes the American product offers twice the protection. What is the sound correction?
questions.answer: The European frame caps the displayed value at 50+ while the United States allows higher numbers, and beyond about SPF 50 the marginal UVB benefit is small, so the difference in labels overstates the difference in protection
questions.distractor: SPF 100 provides twice the protection of SPF 50, so the American product is the stronger choice for a person at high risk of skin cancer
questions.correction: Protection is not linear in the labelled number. An SPF of 50 transmits about one fiftieth of the erythemally effective ultraviolet, and an SPF of 100 about one hundredth, a difference of roughly one percentage point of transmitted dose, which is why the European scheme stops at 50+ rather than advertising larger figures. Applied dose matters far more: at half the tested density of two milligrams per square centimetre, the delivered protection falls well below the label. A learner choosing between markets should compare the UVA signal and the likelihood of applying enough, not the headline number.

questions.prompt: A learner notices that her American sunscreen contains zinc oxide and titanium dioxide while her European one lists bemotrizinol and drometrizole trisiloxane. She concludes the American product is the safer 'physical' option. How should this be assessed?
questions.answer: Both are regulated filter systems with different available molecules, the newer organic filters are permitted in the European Union on the basis of a safety dossier, and no evidence establishes that mineral filters are safer at the population level, so the choice turns on UVA performance, cosmetic acceptability and tolerance
questions.distractor: Mineral filters are chemically inert and therefore safer than organic filters, which enter the bloodstream and disrupt hormones
questions.correction: The United States monograph contains 17 filters against 29 in the European Union, with 18 available only in Europe, and the newer European molecules provide more stable and broader long-wave ultraviolet coverage. The absorption studies that found plasma concentrations above the FDA threshold for five older filters prompted a maximal usage trial framework rather than a finding of harm, and the review of both markets concluded that known human risks of sunscreen appear minimal. Mineral filters are not inert: zinc oxide and titanium dioxide can photocatalyse and are regulated as nanomaterials in some jurisdictions. The defensible selection criteria are measured UVA protection, texture that leads to adequate application, and tolerance of the specific formula.

questions.prompt: A learner develops nail-fold itching, two lifting nail plates and eyelid eczema after switching from lacquer to UV-cured gel. She has a dental appointment for a composite filling next month. What should the appraisal include?
questions.answer: Methacrylate allergy is the leading explanation, the eyelid involvement is consistent with transfer from fingers, patch testing should identify the specific monomer, and the dental exposure makes identification clinically useful rather than cosmetic
questions.distractor: The eyelid eczema must come from eye makeup, because nail products cannot affect skin they never touch, and the dental appointment is unrelated
questions.correction: The nail plate itself is a reasonable barrier, which is why the SCCS accepted HEMA at up to 35 per cent and di-HEMA-TMHDC at up to 99 per cent in UV-cured systems provided the product stays on the plate and off the adjacent skin. Uncured monomer at the cuticle and nail fold is where sensitisation happens, and the hands then transfer it to the eyelids and face, producing dermatitis at a distance. Hydroxyethyl methacrylate sits in the European baseline series for exactly this reason. Because methacrylates cross-react across dental, orthopaedic and cosmetic uses, identifying the sensitiser before a composite filling is placed is practical information for the dentist, not merely a shopping preference.

questions.prompt: A learner's lower lip has had a crusted, non-healing area for eight weeks. She has been exfoliating it with a sugar scrub and applying a peppermint balm. What is the correct response?
questions.answer: A persistent lip lesion needs clinical examination rather than exfoliation, because the differential includes actinic cheilitis and other conditions that a cosmetic routine cannot address, and mechanical irritation may worsen it
questions.distractor: The crust is dead skin from a damaged barrier, so gentle exfoliation twice weekly and a medicated balm will resolve it
questions.correction: The lower lip is a high-accumulation site for ultraviolet exposure and a common location for premalignant and malignant change. A lesion that persists for weeks, bleeds, ulcerates or fails to heal with bland occlusion belongs in a clinical examination, and exfoliating it both delays diagnosis and adds trauma. The lip vermilion has only three to five epithelial layers, no appendages and a weaker lipid barrier, so it is poorly equipped to tolerate scrubs and mentholated products. The non-prescriptive message is to stop the irritants, use plain occlusion and sun protection, and have the lesion looked at.

questions.prompt: A learner reports itching that began three months ago, is generalised, disturbs sleep and is accompanied by unintentional weight loss. She has no rash. What is the correct action?
questions.answer: This combination of chronic generalised pruritus without rash plus systemic symptoms requires prompt medical assessment, because the differential includes haematological, hepatic, renal and endocrine disease
questions.distractor: Generalised itch with no rash is xerosis until proven otherwise, so a twelve-week trial of an occlusive ointment is the appropriate first step
questions.correction: Chronic pruritus on non-lesional skin is a recognised clinical category with a broad systemic differential, and the addition of unintentional weight loss and sleep disturbance raises the level of concern well beyond dry skin. Prevalence estimates of 8 to 25 per cent, and about 25 per cent in people over 65, describe how common the symptom is, not how benign each presentation is. Emollients remain appropriate comfort care, but they are not a diagnostic strategy, and a delayed assessment is the specific harm that lesson 57 described when a cosmetic routine stands in for a clinical question.

questions.prompt: A learner reads that a 'hair growth serum' contains caffeine, biotin and peptides, and that a randomised trial of a low-level laser comb increased terminal hair density. She has patterned thinning at the temples. What is the accurate appraisal?
questions.answer: Patterned thinning with miniaturisation suggests androgenetic alopecia, for which topical minoxidil and oral finasteride are the two FDA-approved drugs, while the serum has no established mechanism for reversing miniaturisation and the laser evidence comes from a network meta-analysis with short follow-up and commercial sponsorship to check
questions.distractor: Because a laser device increased hair density in a randomised trial, the serum and the comb are interchangeable options and the cheapest should be chosen
questions.correction: The 2024 network meta-analysis pooled 17 randomised placebo-controlled trials with at least 20 participants and 24 weeks of follow-up and reported terminal hair density gains of roughly 10 to 19 per cm squared for the better-performing interventions, with the highest-ranked product being a branded formulation and with finasteride, 2 per cent minoxidil and one supplement not statistically separated from placebo in men. That is an evidence map, not a licence to substitute categories. Androgenetic alopecia is a diagnosis made on pattern, family history and hair diameter diversity, and a cosmetic serum containing caffeine and biotin has no trial evidence of reversing miniaturisation. Biotin supplementation also interferes with several immunoassays, which is a reason for caution rather than enthusiasm.

questions.prompt: A learner asks why her dermatologist wants to look at her scalp with a magnifier before deciding about treatment, when the shedding has already been going on for four months. What is the best explanation?
questions.answer: Magnified examination distinguishes hair diameter diversity and miniaturisation from uniform diffuse shedding, which separates pattern loss from telogen effluvium and changes whether treatment is aimed at a chronic androgen-driven process or at recovery from a trigger
questions.distractor: The magnifier is used to check for product residue and poor scalp hygiene, which are the usual causes of shedding
questions.correction: Pattern loss and diffuse shedding look similar to a casual observer and differ in what happens to individual follicles. In androgenetic alopecia, follicles progressively miniaturise, so the scalp shows a widening distribution of hair shaft diameters, and the process is chronic and treatable but not curable. In telogen effluvium the follicles are normal and the shedding follows a trigger by two to three months, with recovery in about 95 per cent of acute cases. Product residue and hygiene are not causes of alopecia, and treating shedding as a cleansing problem delays the distinction that determines the entire management plan.

questions.prompt: A learner has a single dark patch on the cheek that appeared after a healed spot, and a friend tells her it is melasma and that she needs prescription creams. What is the correct appraisal?
questions.answer: A mark confined to the site of previous inflammation is more consistent with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which usually fades over months and does not require hydroquinone, whereas melasma is symmetrical, photodistributed and chronic
questions.distractor: Any dark facial patch is melasma, so prescription-strength lightening should be started before the pigment becomes permanent
questions.correction: Distribution and history carry the diagnosis. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows a recognisable injury at the same site, is often solitary or scattered rather than symmetrical, and resolves as the epidermis turns over, although it can take many months in darker skin. Melasma is bilateral, centred on the cheeks, forehead and upper lip, is driven by ultraviolet and visible light with a hormonal contribution, and relapses. Applying a prescription-strength depigmenting agent to a resolving mark adds irritation and, in darker skin, can produce the very pigmentation it was meant to treat. Where the diagnosis is uncertain, examination is the next step.

questions.prompt: A learner taking amiodarone develops a burning erythema on the face and hands after a bright weekend, and a friend advises her to stop the tablet until the skin settles. What is the correct response?
questions.answer: She should contact the prescriber rather than stop a cardiac medicine, because the reaction is a drug-related phototoxicity that is managed by dose review, photoprotection and clinical monitoring, and amiodarone persists in tissue for a long time after any change
questions.distractor: Stopping the drug immediately is the priority, since removing the photosensitiser is the only reliable way to prevent further reactions
questions.correction: Phototoxicity from amiodarone is well documented, and the drug is highly lipophilic with a very long elimination half-life, so even a prompt change does not remove the photosensitiser from tissue quickly. Stopping an antiarrhythmic without cardiological advice carries a risk of arrhythmia that is far greater than the skin reaction. The cosmetic contribution is real but secondary: broad-spectrum sunscreen, opaque clothing, shade and attention to reflected light reduce exposure, and the drug-sensitivity literature lists the culprit classes so that a learner can raise a specific question with the prescriber rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to test whether a retinoid improves the texture of her right cheek. She plans four two-week periods, alternating the product and a plain moisturiser, with a one-week gap, photographs taken by a friend who does not know the schedule, and a decision rule written down beforehand. What is the main remaining threat to her conclusion?
questions.answer: Carryover: retinoid effects on the epidermis persist for weeks, so a one-week washout may leave activity in the control periods and shrink the observed difference, which biases the test toward finding nothing
questions.distractor: There is no remaining threat, because alternating periods with blinding and a pre-specified rule is the strongest design available and removes all bias
questions.correction: A repeated crossover design is strong for a condition that returns to baseline quickly, and weak where the intervention has a lingering effect. Retinoids alter epidermal turnover and barrier function over weeks, so activity from one period can overlap the next, diluting the contrast. The same logic applies to any product whose effect is structural rather than symptomatic. The honest adaptations are longer washout periods, a longer total duration, or accepting that the design can detect only large differences and stating that limit in advance rather than discovering it after a null result.
